title: Minimum Swaps 2
directAnswer: The array is a permutation of 1..n, so it defines a set of cycles: each element points to the position it belongs in. A cycle of length L needs exactly L − 1 swaps to fix. So the minimum total swaps = sum over all cycles of (cycle_size − 1) = n − (number of cycles). Walk the array once, follow each unvisited cycle to its end, and accumulate. O(n) time, O(n) space for the visited marks.

remember.pattern: Permutation cycle decomposition → n − (number of cycles)
remember.formula:
swaps = 0
visited = [False]*n
for i in range(n):
    if visited[i] or arr[i] == i + 1:
        continue
    size = 0
    j = i
    while not visited[j]:
        visited[j] = True
        j = arr[j] - 1     # follow edge: value v belongs at index v-1
        size += 1
    swaps += size - 1
rules: Values are `1..n`, so the correct index of value `v` is `v - 1`. The edge `i → arr[i] - 1` defines the permutation.
A cycle of length `L` costs exactly `L − 1` swaps — fixing `L − 1` elements snaps the last one into place for free.
Total minimum swaps = `n − (number of cycles)`. Fixed points (`arr[i] == i + 1`) are length-1 cycles costing 0.
Each element is visited **once** across all cycles — that's what makes it `O(n)`, not `O(n²)`.
This only works because the input is a permutation of `1..n` with no duplicates or gaps; otherwise the cycle structure breaks.
whenToUse: Minimum swaps to sort a permutation of consecutive integers
Any 'minimum adjacent-or-arbitrary swaps to reach a target arrangement' where each element has a unique destination
Problems that reduce to following 'this belongs there' pointers — that's a functional graph of cycles
Counting connected components in a permutation
antiSignals: Only **adjacent** swaps are allowed → that's counting inversions (merge sort / BIT), not cycles
Array has duplicates or isn't a clean permutation → no well-defined destination per element; cycle logic fails
You must minimize swaps to a *non-sorted* target → relabel to the target's index space first, then apply cycles
remember.takeaway: A permutation is secretly a graph of cycles, and sorting it is just breaking every cycle. Each length-L cycle needs L−1 swaps, so the answer is n minus the cycle count. Seeing 'array is a permutation → think cycles' unlocks minimum swaps, cyclic sort, and Couples Holding Hands.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that a permutation decomposes into disjoint cycles and that each cycle of length L needs exactly L − 1 swaps — turning a swap-counting puzzle into a graph traversal, rather than simulating swaps blindly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Re-searching the array for the element that belongs at each position (O(n²)), or counting a cycle's cost as its full length L instead of L − 1.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say 'this array is a permutation, so it's a union of cycles; each cycle of length L costs L − 1 swaps, total n − cycles.' Prove the L − 1 with a tiny example and note each index is visited once for O(n).

problemStatement: You are given an unordered array consisting of consecutive integers `[1, 2, 3, …, n]` without any duplicates. You are allowed to swap **any two elements** (not just adjacent ones). Find and return the **minimum number of swaps** required to sort the array in ascending order.
constraints: The array is a permutation of the integers 1..n (each appears exactly once)
Swaps may be between any two positions, not only adjacent ones
understanding: The array is a permutation of 1..n. Sorting it means sending every value v to index v−1. Because any two positions can be swapped, the minimum number of swaps is governed purely by the permutation's cycle structure: each disjoint cycle of length L requires L−1 swaps.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the values guaranteed to be exactly 1..n with no gaps or duplicates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — it's a true permutation. That's essential: it guarantees every value has a unique target index v−1, which is what makes the cycle decomposition well-defined.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I swap any two elements, or only adjacent ones?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any two. If it were adjacent-only, the answer would be the inversion count, a completely different (and larger) quantity.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the array start 1-indexed or 0-indexed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The values are 1..n but stored in a 0-indexed array, so value v belongs at index v−1. Getting this offset right is the crux of the edge formula.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array already possibly sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — then every element is its own fixed point (a length-1 cycle) and the answer is 0 swaps.

examples.explanation: One cycle 0→3→1→2→0 of length 4 → 4 − 1 = 3 swaps. (Following: index 0 holds 4 which belongs at index 3, index 3 holds 2 → index 1, etc.)
Cycle 0→1→2→3→0 of length 4 (cost 3) plus a fixed point at index 4 (value 5, cost 0). Total 3.
Cycles: {0}, {5}, {6} fixed points; and 1→2→4→3→1 of length 4 → 3 swaps. Total 3.

approaches.name: Greedy Selection — Search for the Right Element Each Time
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this to show you can produce a correct, minimal answer by always placing the right value at index i — then point out the inner search makes it O(n²).
hints: Walk left to right. At index i the correct value is i + 1. If it's already there, move on.
If not, find where value i + 1 currently sits and swap it into index i. That fixes index i permanently.
Counting each such swap gives a correct, minimal total — but how expensive is finding the element to swap in each time?
approaches.complexityReasoning: The outer loop visits n indices. For each mismatched index we linearly search the rest of the array for the value that belongs there → up to O(n) per index. Worst case O(n²) time, O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Fix the array one position at a time, left to right. At index `i` the value that belongs there is `i + 1`. If `arr[i]` already equals `i + 1`, it's correct — move on. Otherwise, search the array for the index `k` where `arr[k] == i + 1`, swap `arr[i]` and `arr[k]`, and count one swap. After the swap, index `i` holds its final correct value and is never touched again.

**Why this is minimal.** Every swap we make places at least one element into its permanent correct spot, and we only swap when the current spot is wrong. You can't do better than 'each swap fixes a wrong position', so the count this produces is in fact the minimum — it's the same minimum the cycle method computes, just discovered greedily.

**Why it's the natural first attempt.** It mirrors selection sort: pick the correct element for the current slot and put it there. No theory needed, just 'find the right value and swap it in.'

**Why we don't ship this.** The cost hides in 'search the array for value `i + 1`'. Done naively that's a linear scan per index, giving `O(n²)`. For `n = 10⁵` that's ~10¹⁰ operations — too slow. The fix is to either keep a value→index lookup so the search is `O(1)` (which makes this same greedy approach `O(n)`), or to recognize the cycle structure directly. We present the cycle method as the optimal because it makes the *why* explicit and is the answer interviewers are listening for.
approaches.insight: The greedy 'place the correct element, count the swap' already computes the true minimum — the only inefficiency is re-searching for each element. That observation (replace the linear search with O(1) lookup, or count cycles directly) is the bridge to the linear solution.

approaches.name: Cycle Decomposition (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'the array is a permutation = a union of cycles; each cycle of length L needs L − 1 swaps.'
hints: Think of each index pointing to where its value should go: value arr[i] belongs at index arr[i] − 1. Follow those pointers — what shape do they form?
Starting anywhere and following 'this belongs there' always loops back to where you started: a cycle. The permutation is a disjoint union of such cycles.
A cycle of length L can be sorted with exactly L − 1 swaps. Walk each unvisited cycle once, add (its length − 1), and you're done in O(n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single outer pass over n indices; the inner while-loop follows cycle edges, but every index is marked visited and entered exactly once across all cycles. Total edge follows = n → O(n) time. The visited array is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Treat the array as a function on positions: from index `i`, the value `arr[i]` ultimately belongs at index `arr[i] − 1`, so draw an edge `i → arr[i] − 1`. Because the input is a permutation (a bijection), following these edges from any start always returns to the start — the positions partition into disjoint **cycles**. Sorting the array means turning every cycle into a set of fixed points.

**Why a length-L cycle costs exactly L − 1 swaps.** Take a cycle of `L` misplaced elements. Pick any position in it and swap its element directly into that element's correct home. That single swap puts one element permanently right and shrinks the cycle to length `L − 1` (the displaced element joins the remaining chain). Repeat: each swap removes one more element from the cycle. After `L − 1` swaps, only one element remains, and it is forced into the one empty correct slot for free. You cannot do fewer, because each swap can correctly place at most... well, it permanently fixes one new element per swap, and `L` elements need fixing with the last one free → exactly `L − 1`. Summed over all cycles, the total is `Σ (Lₖ − 1) = n − (number of cycles)`.

**How the traversal works.** Keep a `visited` array. For each index `i` not yet visited, walk the cycle: mark `i`, jump to `j = arr[i] − 1`, mark it, continue until you return to an already-visited node, counting the cycle length as you go. Add `length − 1` to the answer. Fixed points (`arr[i] == i + 1`) are length-1 cycles contributing `0`, so you can skip them outright.

**Why it's O(n).** Every index is marked visited the first time it's touched and never re-entered, so across all cycles the inner loop runs `n` times total — not `n` per index. That's the decisive improvement over the greedy search.

**Why the permutation assumption is load-bearing.** The edge `i → arr[i] − 1` is only a valid permutation (every node has exactly one out-edge and one in-edge) because the values are exactly `1..n` with no repeats. Duplicates or gaps would break the bijection and the cycle decomposition wouldn't hold.
approaches.insight: The reframe is everything: an array that's a permutation *is* a directed graph of disjoint cycles, and 'minimum swaps to sort' is just 'break every cycle'. The cost formula `n − cycles` falls straight out of 'each cycle of length L costs L − 1'. Carry this lens forward — Couples Holding Hands, cyclic sort, and 'minimum operations to make identical permutations' are all the same cycle-counting in disguise.

dryRun.intro: Follow edges i → arr[i] − 1, marking visited; add (cycle length − 1).

code.python:
def minimumSwaps(self, arr: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(arr)
    visited: list[bool] = [False] * n
    swaps = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if visited[i] or arr[i] == i + 1:
            continue
        cycle_size = 0
        j = i
        while not visited[j]:
            visited[j] = True
            j = arr[j] - 1
            cycle_size += 1
        swaps += cycle_size - 1
    return swaps

java.explanation: Skip nodes already part of a counted cycle, and fixed points (length-1 cycles cost 0).
Start walking the cycle from this unvisited index.
Follow the permutation edge: value arr[j] belongs at index arr[j] − 1.
Count nodes in this cycle as we mark them visited.
A length-L cycle needs exactly L − 1 swaps to resolve.

python.explanation: Skip visited indices and fixed points — they contribute nothing.
Begin the cycle walk at index i.
Hop to where the current value belongs — the cycle's next node.
Add the cycle's cost; total becomes n − (number of cycles).

pitfalls: Counting cycle length L as the cost instead of L − 1 — overcounts by the number of cycles.
Forgetting the value→index offset (using arr[j] instead of arr[j] − 1 to follow the edge).
Re-entering already-visited cycles because you didn't mark or check visited — degrades correctness and time.

commonMistakes: Re-searching the array for each element's correct value, making it O(n²).
Charging a cycle of length L as L swaps instead of L − 1.
Confusing this 'any swap' problem with the adjacent-swap (inversion-count) variant.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting L instead of L − 1 per cycle
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The last element of a cycle drops into place for free once the others are fixed. Charging the full length L over-counts by exactly the number of cycles.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: swaps += cycleSize;        // over-counts every cycle by 1
commonMistakesDetailed.good: swaps += cycleSize - 1;    // last element falls into place free

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong edge: forgetting the −1 offset
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Values are 1..n but indices are 0..n−1. Value v belongs at index v − 1, so the cycle edge is arr[j] − 1. Using arr[j] walks the wrong graph and miscounts cycles.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: j = arr[j]        # off-by-one: treats value as index
commonMistakesDetailed.good: j = arr[j] - 1    # value v belongs at index v - 1

patternNote: Permutation Cycle Decomposition. Recognise it whenever the array is a permutation and you need minimum arbitrary swaps to sort: build the functional graph i → arr[i] − 1, count disjoint cycles, and the answer is n − cycles (each cycle of length L costs L − 1). Same lens as cyclic sort, Couples Holding Hands, and Set Mismatch.
